text:
310. A pupil and a teacher. The pupil will not let anything be explained to him, for he continually interrupts with doubts—for instance as to the existence of things, the meaning of words, and so on. The teacher says "Stop interrupting me and do as I tell you. So far your doubts don't make sense at all."

311. Or imagine that the boy questioned the truth of historical claims (and everything that connects up with them)—and even whether the earth had existed at all a hundred years before.

312. Here it strikes me as if this doubt were hollow. But in that case—isn't belief in history hollow too? No; there is so much that this connects up with.

313. So is that what makes us believe a proposition? Well—the grammar of "believe" does hang together with the grammar of the proposition believed. The connection between believing and the proposition believed is not accidental. The structure of belief reflects the structure of what is believed. When we say we believe some proposition, the way we use "believe" presupposes that we understand the proposition in question according to a certain grammar. The grammar of "I believe the earth existed a hundred years ago" is parasitic on the grammar of "the earth existed a hundred years ago."

314. Imagine that the schoolboy really did ask "and is there a table there even when I turn round, and even when no one is there to see it?" Is the teacher to reassure him—and say "of course there is!"? Perhaps the teacher will get a bit impatient, but think that the boy will grow out of asking such questions.

315. That is to say, the teacher will feel that this is not really a legitimate question at all. And it would be just the same if the pupil cast doubt on the uniformity of nature, that is to say on the justification of inductive arguments.—The teacher would feel that this was only holding them up, that this way the pupil would only get stuck and make no progress.—And he would be right. It would be as if someone were looking for some object in a room; he opens a drawer and doesn't see it there; then he closes it again, waits, and opens it once more to see if perhaps it isn't there now, and keeps on like that. He has not learned to look for things. And in the same way this pupil has not learned how to ask questions. He has not learned the game that we are trying to teach him. The teacher's impatience reflects a recognition that the pupil's doubt obstructs the very process by which one learns. To doubt the uniformity of nature while trying to learn empirical methods is not to exercise healthy skepticism—it is to fail to understand what empirical inquiry consists in. The person who repeatedly opens the drawer has not grasped what searching involves. Similarly, the pupil who doubts induction has not yet grasped what it is to learn from experience.

316. And isn't it the same as if the pupil were to hold up his history lesson with doubts as to whether the earth really existed a hundred years ago?

317. This doubt isn't one of the doubts in our game. (But not as if we chose this game!) The exclusion of certain doubts from our practice is not arbitrary, yet neither is it a matter of choice in any ordinary sense. We did not convene and decide to exclude radical skeptical doubts about the past or about induction. Rather, these doubts fall outside the structure of the practice itself. They are not moves within the game but rejections of the game's framework.

318. "The question doesn't arise at all." Its answer would characterize a method. But there is no sharp boundary between methodological propositions and propositions within a method. Whether the earth existed a hundred years ago is not a question that arises within historical inquiry. The answer to such a question—if we were to give one—would not be a historical finding but a specification of what historical inquiry presupposes. It would characterize the method rather than employ it. Yet the boundary between such methodological propositions and ordinary empirical propositions is not sharp.

319. But wouldn't one have to say then, that there is no sharp boundary between propositions of logic and empirical propositions? The lack of sharpness is that of the boundary between rule and empirical proposition. If methodological propositions shade into empirical ones, and if logical propositions are among those that characterize methods, then it follows that logic and empirical content are not sharply divided. The vagueness here is the vagueness of the distinction between rules and descriptions.

320. Here one must, I believe, remember that the concept 'proposition' itself is not a sharp one. Part of the difficulty in drawing these boundaries stems from the fact that "proposition" is not a precisely delimited concept. We use it to cover statements that function in diverse ways—as expressions of empirical claims, as stipulations, as rules, as definitions.

321. Isn't what I am saying: any empirical proposition can be transformed into a postulate—and then becomes a norm of description. But I am suspicious even of this. The sentence is too general. One almost wants to say "any empirical proposition can, theoretically, be transformed…" but what does "theoretically" mean here? It sounds all too reminiscent of the Tractatus. One is tempted to claim that any empirical proposition could in principle be elevated to the status of a methodological rule—could be treated as a norm that structures our descriptions rather than as a description itself. Yet this formulation is suspect. The word "theoretically" suggests a mere logical possibility detached from actual practice, as though we could survey all possible uses from some neutral standpoint. Whether a proposition can function as a norm is not determined by theoretical considerations but by its role in our actual methods of investigation.

322. What if the pupil refused to believe that this mountain had been there beyond human memory? We should say that he had no grounds for this suspicion.

323. So rational suspicion must have grounds? We might also say: "the reasonable man believes this." Suspicion is rational only when it has grounds—when there is some reason, some evidence or consideration, that supports it. The pupil who doubts the mountain's antiquity without grounds does not exhibit rational doubt. We express this by appealing to what the reasonable person believes.

324. Thus we should not call anybody reasonable who believed something in despite of scientific evidence. Reasonableness is constrained by evidence, particularly by well-established scientific evidence. To believe in defiance of such evidence is to place oneself outside the community of rational inquiry.

325. When we say that we know that such and such…, we mean that any reasonable person in our position would also know it, that it would be a piece of unreason to doubt it. Thus Moore too wants to say not merely that he knows that he has two hands, etc., but also that anyone endowed with reason in his position would know it just the same. The claim to know something is implicitly general. It is not merely a report of one's own psychological state but an assertion about what is knowable given certain circumstances. To say "I know" is to say that the grounds for knowledge are available, that doubt would be unreasonable.

326. But who says what it is reasonable to believe in this situation? This question threatens to undermine the appeal to reasonableness by suggesting that reasonableness itself is arbitrary or conventional. Yet the question misconstrues the nature of the appeal. Reasonableness is not determined by fiat but is manifest in our practices.

327. So it might be said: "The reasonable man believes: that the earth has been there since long before his birth, that his life has been spent on the surface of the earth, or near it, that he has never, for example, been on the moon, that he has a nervous system and various innards like all other people, etc., etc." We can enumerate beliefs characteristic of the reasonable person. These are not beliefs adopted on the basis of explicit reasoning but beliefs that frame reasoning. They constitute part of the background against which inquiry proceeds.

328. "I know it as I know that my name is L. W."

329. 'If he calls that in doubt—whatever "doubt" means here—he will never learn this game.' Certain pieces of knowledge are so fundamental to our practice that to doubt them is to exclude oneself from the practice. If someone doubts his own name, or whether he has ever been on the moon in the absence of any reason to think he has, then he has not grasped the framework within which knowledge-claims are made and assessed.

330. So here the sentence "I know…" expresses the readiness to believe certain things. To say "I know" is to express not just a cognitive state but a stance—a readiness to proceed on the basis of certain beliefs, to treat them as fixed points.

331. If we ever do act with certainty on the strength of belief, should we wonder that there is much we cannot doubt? Action requires certainty about many things. To act is to take certain propositions as settled. Doubt that extends to everything paralyzes action and inquiry alike.

332. Imagine that someone were to say, without wanting to philosophize, "I don't know if I have ever been on the moon; I don't remember ever having been there." (Why would this person be so radically different from us?) In the first place—how would he know that he was on the moon? How does he imagine it? Compare: "I do not know if I was ever in the village of X." But neither could I say that if X were in Turkey, for I know that I was never in Turkey. The person who says he doesn't know whether he has been on the moon betrays a misunderstanding of what it would be to have been on the moon. Going to the moon is not an event one could forget in the way one forgets a brief visit to a village. The comparison with the village in Turkey reveals this: I can be uncertain about visits to nearby villages, but not about whether I have been to countries I have never visited.

333. I ask someone "Have you ever been in China?" He replies "I don't know." Here one would surely say "You don't know? Have you any reason to believe you might have been there at some time? Were you for example ever near the Chinese border? Or were your parents there at the time when you were going to be born?"—Normally Europeans do know whether they have been in China or not. The answer "I don't know" to the question about China is so anomalous that it demands explanation. Under what circumstances could a person fail to know whether he had been in China? Only under very specific and unusual ones—perhaps if he had been near the border and couldn't be sure whether he crossed it, or if his early childhood included travel he cannot now remember. Absent such special circumstances, the claim not to know is unintelligible.

334. That is to say: only in such-and-such circumstances does a reasonable person doubt that. Reasonable doubt is circumstance-dependent. What it makes sense to doubt varies with the situation.

335. The procedure in a court of law rests on the fact that circumstances give statements a certain probability. The statement that, for example, someone came into the world without parents wouldn't ever be taken into consideration there. Legal proceedings illustrate how doubt is constrained by background assumptions. Courts assess the probability of claims relative to circumstances, but certain propositions are excluded from consideration altogether—not because they have been disproven but because they fall outside the framework of reasonable doubt. The claim that someone was born without parents is not rejected on evidential grounds in a court; it is excluded as falling outside the space of live possibilities.
